name: H-6
tagline: China's long-serving twin-engine jet bomber, still in production. Tracing its lineage to the Soviet Tupolev Tu-16 'Badger', heavily re-engineered variants like the H-6K and H-6N remain in front-line production nearly seven decades after its first flight.
history: China acquired a license to build the Tupolev Tu-16 under a 1957 Sino-Soviet agreement, and the first Soviet-supplied-kit Tu-16 (redesignated H-6) flew in China on 27 September 1959; a fully indigenously produced airframe followed on 24 December 1968 after the Sino-Soviet split forced China to reverse-engineer the type from limited technical assistance. The original H-6A became China's first nuclear-capable bomber, dropping the country's first live nuclear device during a 1965 test, and later variants added maritime-strike missiles (H-6D/G), tanker conversions (HY-6/H-6U) and, from the 2000s, a wholesale modernisation program. The H-6K, first flown in January 2007 and in service from around 2009, replaced the original Soviet-derived turbojets with Soloviev D-30KP-2 turbofans, dramatically improving range and efficiency, and added a glass cockpit plus six underwing hardpoints for long-range CJ-10/CJ-20 land-attack and YJ-12 anti-ship cruise missiles, effectively turning the H-6 into a stand-off missile truck. The H-6N, which emerged around 2018-2019, went further still: it added a fixed aerial-refuelling probe and a modified fuselage with a semi-recessed weapons station able to carry a single large air-launched ballistic missile, restoring a credible air leg to China's nuclear triad pending the future H-20 stealth bomber. China publicly showcased H-6N aerial refuelling from Y-20U tankers for the first time in 2025, and H-6K/H-6N units have flown repeated joint long-range patrols with Russian Tu-95 bombers near Japan, Korea and Alaska since 2019, along with frequent sorties near Taiwan and over the South China Sea.

range.text: ~3,730 mi (6,000 km) ferry range; ~2,175 mi (3,500 km) combat radius claimed for H-6K (estimated)

specifications.engines: 2 x Soloviev/Aviadvigatel D-30KP-2 turbofans (~27,000 lbf / 118 kN each) on H-6K/H-6N variants; earlier H-6A/H-6M variants used Xian WP8 turbojets (license-built Mikulin RD-3M derivatives)
specifications.armament: Up to 6 x CJ-10/CJ-20 land-attack cruise missiles or YJ-12 supersonic anti-ship cruise missiles on underwing pylons (H-6K); YJ-21 hypersonic anti-ship ballistic missile (H-6K/H-6J); single JL-1 or CH-AS-X-13 air-launched ballistic missile on a semi-recessed station (H-6N, nuclear-capable); free-fall bombs up to ~26,000 lb; earlier variants carried defensive 23mm NR-23 cannon turrets, largely deleted on modern missile-carrier variants

unitCost.text: ~$60M (estimated for modernized H-6K; China does not publish official unit costs)

variants.desc: Original 1960s nuclear-capable bomber, China's first aircraft cleared to deliver a nuclear weapon; used for China's early nuclear tests.
Maritime strike variants armed with anti-ship cruise missiles (C-601 and later YJ-8/YJ-12 family).
Dedicated aerial-refuelling tanker conversions supporting PLAAF/PLANAF fighter and bomber operations.

Major 2000s modernisation with Western-derived D-30KP-2 turbofans, glass cockpit, and six external hardpoints for long-range CJ-10/CJ-20 land-attack and YJ-12 anti-ship cruise missiles; the backbone of today's conventional H-6 fleet.
Navy (PLANAF) maritime strike derivative of the H-6K with additional payload for anti-ship missions.
Air-refuellable, nuclear-capable variant with a fixed refuelling probe and semi-recessed belly station for a single large air-launched ballistic missile, restoring China's nuclear air leg.

flightradar24.howToFind: H-6 sorties are essentially invisible on Flightradar24 since the type does not broadcast civil ADS-B; public awareness of individual flights - such as long-range patrols near Japan, Taiwan or Alaska - comes almost entirely from allied military press releases (e.g. Japan's JASDF, Taiwan's MND) and satellite imagery rather than crowd-sourced flight trackers.

quickFacts: The H-6 is a Chinese-built descendant of the Soviet Tu-16 that first flew in 1952 - and China has kept it not just alive but growing.
The newest H-6N carries an air-launched ballistic missile semi-recessed under its belly and can refuel in flight.
H-6Ks now routinely fly around Taiwan and out past the First Island Chain - the most visible instrument of Chinese air power signalling.
Its modern D-30 turbofans and glass cockpit make the H-6K essentially a new bomber wearing a 1950s shape.
China is the only nation still building a Tu-16 lineage aircraft - seven decades after the original's first flight.

overview: The Xian H-6 is a Chinese twin-engine strategic bomber, originally a licence-built copy of the Soviet Tupolev Tu-16 'Badger'. China began building it under licence in the late 1950s, with full domestic production established by 1968.{{ref:wiki-h6}}

Modern H-6K and H-6N variants have been extensively re-engined and re-equipped to carry long-range cruise missiles and, in the H-6N, a single large air-launched ballistic missile, making a decades-old airframe a modern stand-off strike platform. H-6s fly frequent patrols and exercises around Taiwan and through the Western Pacific.{{ref:dsa-h6}}{{ref:nsj-h6}}

sections.heading: Origins & Concept
paragraphs: The H-6 story starts in Moscow: China received Tu-16 pattern aircraft and licence rights in the late 1950s, flying its first Xian-assembled example in 1959 before the Sino-Soviet split cut off support. Chinese industry spent the 1960s painfully mastering the type alone - the program that taught China to build big jets - with full domestic production maturing by 1968.{{ref:wiki-h6}}

For its first decades the H-6 did what Badgers did: free-fall bombs, including China's early airdropped nuclear tests, plus naval variants lobbing first-generation anti-ship missiles. It was already dated in 1970; nobody then imagined the airframe's fourth act.{{ref:wiki-h6}}

sections.heading: Development
paragraphs: The 2007 H-6K was effectively a new bomber in old clothes: Russian D-30 turbofans replacing thirsty turbojets (later domestically substituted), a solid nose with modern radar replacing the glazed bombardier station, glass cockpit, reduced crew - and the whole airframe rebuilt as a carrier for six CJ-20 land-attack cruise missiles with reach beyond 1,500 km.{{ref:wiki-h6}}

The family kept branching: the H-6J for naval aviation with supersonic YJ-12 anti-ship missiles, the H-6G jammer/support types, tanker versions - and the H-6N of 2019, with an aerial-refuelling probe and a recessed belly built around a single enormous air-launched ballistic missile widely assessed as carrying a hypersonic glider or anti-ship warhead. That variant gives China an air leg of its nuclear triad for the first time in decades.{{ref:dsa-h6}}

sections.heading: Service History
paragraphs: The modern H-6's beat is coercive presence: near-daily appearances in Taiwan's air-defence identification zone, encirclement exercises rehearsing blockade strikes, long loops through the Bashi Channel and Miyako Strait into the Philippine Sea, and joint bomber patrols with Russian Tu-95s that have brushed Alaska's air-defence zone - each flight a signal calibrated for its audience.{{ref:ni-taiwan}}

Its combat record is thin by design - decades of deterrence patrols rather than strikes, with the type's live employment limited to Cold War-era nuclear tests and border-war support - but its operational tempo is the opposite: among Chinese military aircraft, none appears in more foreign defence-ministry press releases than the H-6.{{ref:wiki-h6}}

sections.heading: Design & Engineering
paragraphs: The Tu-16 bones remain visible: shoulder-mounted swept wings, engines buried in the wing roots, area-ruled 'coke bottle' rear fuselage. What changed is everything that matters for a missile truck - propulsion economy for long patrols, sensors to find and cue targets at range, hardpoints stressed for six two-tonne missiles, and datalinks tying the bomber into China's reconnaissance-strike web of satellites and over-the-horizon radars.{{ref:wiki-h6}}

The design's persistence is doctrine made metal: when the weapon flies 1,500+ km, the launcher needs endurance and payload, not stealth or speed. It is the same conclusion that keeps the B-52 flying - reached independently, from the same 1950s generation of airframes.{{ref:nsj-h6}}

sections.heading: Current Status & Outlook
paragraphs: The H-6 is the longest industrial apprenticeship in aviation paying off: the program that taught China heavy aircraft construction now fields the missiles-first bomber doctrine everyone else is copying, while its true successor - the stealthy flying-wing H-20 - remains perpetually 'soon'. Until it arrives, the Badger's grandchildren are the Pacific's bomber reality.{{ref:ni-taiwan}}

Seven decades after the Tu-16's first flight, the Chinese lineage remains in active production and use even though the original Soviet Badgers have long been retired - a pattern also seen with the B-52 and Tu-95.{{ref:nsj-h6}}

accidentsAndIncidents.title: Mid-air collision, emergency landing at Cangxian
accidentsAndIncidents.summary: During a joint training exercise, a J-6 fighter collided with an H-6's tail, severing its vertical stabiliser and jamming the elevator. The crew flew the crippled bomber roughly 3,000 metres and landed it safely; all aboard both aircraft survived.

accidentsAndIncidents.title: Shot down over the Persian Gulf
accidentsAndIncidents.summary: An Iraqi Air Force H-6D on an anti-ship mission was shot down by an Iranian F-14 firing a Phoenix missile and crashed into the Persian Gulf, killing all six aboard.

accidentsAndIncidents.title: Runway overrun and breakup at Fenyang
accidentsAndIncidents.summary: A PLAAF H-6 touched down fast on landing at an airfield in Shanxi Province and could not stop, running off the runway and breaking into three sections. All six occupants escaped.
